items.value: Only assumption 1 (that global warming is causing an earlier and longer spring) is implied; assumption 2 about harm to bird populations is not
items.reasoning: The passage reports that warmer winters with less snow produce a longer lag between spring events and a more protracted vernal window, and that ice melts earlier — so the account rests on an unstated premise that this warming (i.e. global warming) is driving an earlier, longer spring. Assumption 1 therefore holds. Assumption 2 does not: the passage says only that the birds do not return, and presents that as a cause of delay or lengthening in springtime ecological events; it makes no claim, explicit or presupposed, about whether the change is good or bad for bird populations. The consequences it does name are for agriculture, fisheries and tourism.

items.value: Raising nitrogen use efficiency is essential for both food production and the environment
items.reasoning: The passage sets two facts against each other: synthetic nitrogen is needed for the high yields that feed more than half the world's population, yet only about 40 per cent of applied nitrogen reaches the harvested crop while 60 per cent is lost as nitrous oxide and eutrophying runoff. The only message that reconciles both is to use nitrogen more efficiently. B takes just the food half and C, D take just the environment half; and neither replacing crops nor replacing conventional agriculture is mentioned anywhere in the text.

items.value: Climate justice should be written in detail into the rules of new climate compacts and agreements
items.reasoning: The passage says climate justice is a significant principle that has so far eluded consensus in climate summits and compacts, and that the crucial question ahead is how resources, technologies and regulations are used to support victims — including adaptation support and compensation for loss and damage. That is a call to embed climate justice in the rules of climate agreements, which is A. B (uneven distribution of resources) and D (blaming developed countries) state positions the passage never takes; C names climate refugees and huge numbers, neither of which appears in the text, and is a fragment of the message rather than its crux.

Half-yearly compounding for one year gives Q = P(1 + R/200)^2 = P(1 + R/100 + R^2/40000); annual compounding gives Q = P(1 + S/100). Equating, S/100 = R/100 + R^2/40000, so S exceeds R by R^2/400 whenever R is positive. Numerically, R = 10% compounded half-yearly grows P by a factor 1.05^2 = 1.1025, which needs S = 10.25% annually — so R < S.

If dividing 1186 by n leaves remainder 31, then n divides 1186 - 31 = 1155 and n must exceed the remainder, so n > 31. Since 1155 = 3 x 5 x 7 x 11 it has sixteen divisors: 1, 3, 5, 7, 11, 15, 21, 33, 35, 55, 77, 105, 165, 231, 385, 1155. Nine of these are greater than 31 — 33, 35, 55, 77, 105, 165, 231, 385 and 1155 — and each does leave remainder 31, so the count is 9.

items.value: Both statements are correct: p has 5 possible values and q has 6
items.reasoning: pp + qq + rr = 11(p + q + r), and a 3-digit number of the form tt0 is 110t, so p + q + r = 10t. As the digits are distinct and lie in 1-9, the sum lies between 6 and 24, forcing t = 1 or 2, i.e. p + q + r = 10 or 20. The eight triples with p < q < r are (1,2,7), (1,3,6), (1,4,5), (2,3,5) summing to 10 and (3,8,9), (4,7,9), (5,6,9), (5,7,8) summing to 20. The smallest members give p in {1,2,3,4,5} — five values — and the middle members give q in {2,3,4,6,7,8} — six values. Both statements hold.

To be below 2000 the thousands digit must be 1, so the other three places are a permutation of 2, 3 and 4 — six numbers in all. The thousands place contributes 6 x 1000 = 6000, and in each of the hundreds, tens and units places each of 2, 3, 4 appears twice, contributing 2(2 + 3 + 4) = 18 per place. The total is 6000 + 1800 + 180 + 18 = 7998, which matches direct addition of 1234, 1243, 1324, 1342, 1423 and 1432.

A block of 10 consecutive objects read clockwise round a circle of 12 is fixed entirely by where it starts, and there are 12 possible starting positions, all giving distinct selections. Equivalently, leaving out 10 consecutive objects leaves 2 consecutive objects, and the number of ways to pick 2 adjacent objects in a circle of 12 is also 12. The answer 66 is the unrestricted count 12C10 and ignores the consecutiveness condition.

Only the remainder of 10^10 on division by 7 matters. Since 10 leaves remainder 3, and 3^6 leaves remainder 1, 10^10 behaves like 3^10 = 3^6 x 3^4, which reduces to 3^4 = 81, leaving remainder 4. Counting four days on from Sunday gives Thursday. Note the item's wording is loose: if one instead counts today itself as the first day, the shift is 3 and the answer would be Wednesday, which is also offered as an option — the reading taken here is the usual one, that the 10^10th day is 10^10 days after today.

Green and red last equally long, so a signal's full green-to-green cycle is twice its green-to-red time: 50, 78 and 120 seconds respectively. They turn green together again after the LCM of these. With 50 = 2 x 5^2, 78 = 2 x 3 x 13 and 120 = 2^3 x 3 x 5, the LCM is 2^3 x 3 x 5^2 x 13 = 7800 seconds = 130 minutes = 2 hours 10 minutes. Added to 2:00 p.m. this gives 4:10 p.m. Using the one-way times 25, 39, 60 instead would wrongly halve the interval.

items.value: Agroecosystems should be developed in addition to, or alongside, conventional agriculture
items.reasoning: The passage's own framing is additive: sourcing food from uncultivated systems such as forests, wetlands and pastures 'in addition to agricultural lands' lets communities feed themselves year-round and gives a safety net when crops fail or between harvests. D reproduces exactly that additive relationship. A (replacing other trees) and C (converting wastelands) prescribe actions the passage never mentions, and B asserts that conventional agriculture cannot ensure food security — a rejection the passage does not make, since it treats forest foods as a complement, not a substitute.

items.value: Proper effluent treatment protocols must be put in place
items.reasoning: The passage isolates one neglected cause — antibiotics-manufacturing companies not treating their waste — and states that pollution from these factories is fuelling drug-resistant infections near the plants. The practical remedy that follows directly is proper effluent treatment. B is a vague generality that does not address manufacturing waste; C concedes defeat, contradicting the passage's implied call to act on a known and fixable source; and D merely relocates the untreated effluent rather than treating it.

items.value: India needs to invest in universal quality education if it is to hold its own globally
items.reasoning: The passage argues that benefits accrue only when students leave school having acquired gateway skills, that an uneducated workforce will leave the country unable to keep pace with the global economy, and that without a strong primary foundation there can be no improvement in higher education or skill development. A captures that chain. C is directly contradicted, since the passage locates the priority at the foundational level rather than in higher education; B asserts a failure to promote the knowledge economy that the passage never claims; D introduces illiterate parents, who are not mentioned at all. A's phrase 'global power' is slightly stronger than the passage's 'keep pace with the global economy', which is why this is not rated HIGH.

The kth pass advances the ring by k places, so after k passes the holder is child number 1 + k(k+1)/2, counted modulo 40. The ring is back with child-1 when k(k+1)/2 is a multiple of 40, i.e. when k(k+1) is a multiple of 80. Testing k = 1 upward, the triangular numbers reduce mod 40 to 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28, 36, 5, 15, 26, 38, 11, 25 and finally 0 at k = 15, where 15 x 16/2 = 120 = 3 x 40. So 15 passes are needed. The parenthetical 'including child-1' is ambiguous and could be read as counting holders rather than passes, which would give 16.

The letters run backwards from Z to A with Z appearing twice, Y three times, X four times and so on, so the kth block is the letter numbered 27 - k and occurs k + 1 times; the final block, A, occurs 27 times. The total length is the sum of 2 through 27, which is 377, so the middle term is the 189th. Cumulative counts reach 170 at the end of the 17th block and 189 at the end of the 18th, so the 189th term lies in block 18, whose letter is the 9th of the alphabet — I.

items.value: The question cannot be answered even by using both statements together
items.reasoning: Statement-1 only says p and q share a sign: p = 2, q = 1 gives yes while p = 1, q = 2 gives no, so it is insufficient. Statement-2 only says p has the larger magnitude: p = 2, q = 1 gives yes while p = -2, q = 1 gives no, so it too is insufficient. Taken together they still fail, because both conditions hold for p = 2, q = 1 (where p > q) and equally for p = -3, q = -2, where the product 6 is positive and 9 > 4 yet p is smaller than q. The answer flips with the common sign, so option D as printed applies.

items.value: Both statements together are needed, and they settle it: p + q - r is not greater than p - q + r
items.reasoning: Cancelling p from both sides, the question reduces to whether q - r exceeds r - q, that is whether q > r. Statement-1 gives p > q but leaves r free — with p = 5, q = 3 the answer is yes if r = 1 and no if r = 10 — so it is insufficient; Statement-2 gives p < r but leaves q free, and is insufficient for the same reason. Together they chain to r > p > q, so q < r and the required inequality is definitively false. A definite 'no' is an answer, so option C as printed applies.

items.value: Statement-2 alone answers it (150 attended); Statement-1 alone does not
items.reasoning: Tea or coffee covers 75 + 60 - 15 = 120 people. Milk drinkers take no tea but may take coffee, so those who take milk with coffee are already inside the 120 and only the milk-only group adds to the total: total = 120 + (milk only). Statement-1 fixes the milk total at 50 but not how many of them also took coffee, so the total could be anywhere from 120 to 170 — insufficient. Statement-2 gives total = 5 x (milk only); substituting total = 120 + x yields 5x = 120 + x, so x = 30 and the total is 150 — sufficient on its own. Hence exactly one statement suffices.

items.value: The number cannot be determined even from both statements together
items.reasoning: The only digit triple whose sum equals its product is 1, 2, 3, so Statement-1 narrows the number to one of 123, 132, 213, 231, 312, 321 but cannot single one out. Statement-2 alone is satisfied by a great many 3-digit numbers, so it is far weaker. Combining them, the digit sum is 6, and divisibility by 6 requires an even last digit, which leaves two candidates, 132 and 312 — both genuinely divisible by 6. Two survivors means no unique number, so option D as printed applies.

items.value: Either statement alone answers it: the youngest is 4 years old
items.reasoning: With successive ages differing by 2, the five ages are a, a + 2, a + 4, a + 6 and a + 8. Statement-1 gives a + 8 = 3a, so 2a = 8 and a = 4. Statement-2 gives the mean, which for this evenly spaced set is the middle age a + 4, so a + 4 = 8 and again a = 4. Each statement pins the youngest child's age by itself, so option B as printed applies.
